Physical challenge helps because the body gives immediate information back. A run, drill, or climb keeps asking for adjustment, so attention has something real to answer. That is why movement can feel rewarding from inside the act rather than only after the result.

The chapter then widens beyond athletics. Bodily intimacy, yoga, martial arts, seeing, music, and taste can all become richer when sensation is organized by attention instead of left passive. Pleasure still matters, but the chapter keeps pleasure distinct from bodily flow.

The body therefore becomes one of the clearest places where attention learns challenge, rhythm, and response. That prepares the bridge into Chapter 6, where thought becomes the next domain of flow.

That is why the chapter closes by treating bodily flow as more than athletics or pleasure. It is a broader pattern in which sensation becomes shaped by skill, rhythm, challenge, and cultivated notice before Chapter 6 turns to thought.
